name: Tegem
confidence_why: Sosal 2018, the only phonological study of Tegem, documents six contrastive lexical tone patterns with minimal pairs (and reports that Schadeberg 1981 likewise found four tone types), while the sole dissent, Tucker and Bryan 1966 repeating Stevenson's group-level remark that dynamic stress outweighs pitch across the Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa languages, gives no Lafofa data, no placement, and admits that very little is known about Lafofa.

catalog_quote: The lexical tones in Table 10 indicate that Tegem is a tone language, i.e., tones are used to create lexical distinctions while affixation is used for grammatical distinction. The language most frequently uses the two level tones (H/L) and then the two contour tones (F/R). The other two contour tones (FR/RF) are used occasionally and they contrast with the other two contour tones, e.g., FR in ʈîí ‘pile of soil’ and F in ʈíì ‘kind of grass’; RF in ʈǐìl ‘cowbird’ and R in ʈìíl ‘acacia wood’. The tone domain (TBU: tone-bearing unit) in Tegem is the syllable as change of one syllable tone changes the word meaning, i.e., ‘in a tone language each syllable of a word will have its own tone.’ (Dixon 2009:279). ... [sec. 5.5, p. 77] In Tegem, there are lexical tones. For a detailed account of tones in Tegem a post-lexical phonological study is required, i.e. to determine tonal behaviour beyond word level
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tegem (Lafofa) is described as a lexical tone language (H, L, falling, rising; FR/RF on long/extra-long vowels; syllable = TBU). The thesis, the only modern phonological description, says nothing at all about word stress or accent. The only stress remark in the literature reachable here is Stevenson's group-level observation (via Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 18a sec. 2b, covering Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa together) that 'dynamic stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages' -- with no stress position given and nothing specific to Lafofa.
new_statements.exceptions: None; tone/length alternations under suffixation of -go / -i ('this') noted (p. 60); disyllabic noun roots disallow two contour tones or two different level tones (Table 11).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (elicited citation forms of lexical items from two main consultants, one from Tekeim village, one from the Eliri plain villages near Lafofa; recorded in Khartoum). Author explicitly defers post-lexical/phrasal tonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Sosal 2018 describes Tegem (endonym; = Lafofa of Stevenson/Ethnologue, ISO laf, Glottolog lafo1243; Glottolog 5.x places it under a 'Tegem' node tege1244). Data from two main consultants, one from Jebel Tekeim (the 'Jebel Tekeim' dialect of older sources) and one from the Eliri plain villages near Lafofa village, recorded in Khartoum; author treats Tekeim/Lafofa differences as sub-phonemic. El Amira (amir1234-type variety, 'Amira') is explicitly excluded as a separate language. The Tucker & Bryan / Stevenson stress remark is group-level (Koalib-Moro + Talodi-Masakin + Lafofa), not Lafofa-specific.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Tegem as a tone language with no stress statement (Sosal 2018, secs 4.4 and 5.5). Tucker & Bryan add, at group level and via Stevenson, that dynamic stress accompanied by H/L tone exists and 'plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such' -- a stress statement the catalog lacks, but with no placement, no Lafofa-specific data, and an explicit admission that very little is known about Lafofa. Compatible (Sosal never discusses stress), so 'refines' rather than 'contradicts'; the tension between 'stress greater than pitch' and Sosal's 4-6-tone system is noted under conflicts.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa languages taken together, Tucker & Bryan report (second-hand, from Stevenson 1956-57) that dynamic stress, carried on a High or Low tone, matters more than pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in every language of the group; tone is only partly investigated and a few lexical tone doublets exist (none cited for Lafofa). No statement of where stress falls; examples are unmarked for tone and stress; the chapter itself says 'Very little is known about LAFOFA'.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'not equally prominent in all languages'; nothing specific to Lafofa.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan ch. 18a treats Lafofa (L) as a 'Single Unit' alongside the Koalib-Moro and Talodi-Masakin groups; the stress sentence is a group-level generalisation drawn from Stevenson, not a description of Lafofa/Tegem specifically. Sosal 2018 (already on the record) states 'Tegem (or Lafofa as it is known in the literature)' and describes the Tekeim and Eliri-plain varieties.

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone on every syllable: two level tones (high, low) and four contours (falling, rising, falling-rising, rising-falling), the contours analysable as H/L sequences; nothing on word stress.

readall_conflicts: Mild tension, not a contradiction: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (quoting Stevenson 1956-57) say for the K-M/T-M/Lafofa group that dynamic stress 'plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such', whereas Sosal 2018 (the only Lafofa-specific phonology, on the record already) finds Tegem to be a tone language with H, L, F, R (+FR, RF) lexical tones and never mentions stress. Tucker & Bryan hedge ('not equally prominent in all languages', 'Very little is known about LAFOFA', examples unmarked), give no Lafofa examples and no placement, so their statement does not overturn the catalog's reading; the Tegem-specific description wins.
